posts.title: 除了交叉熵，LM Loss还有什么选择？ (Beyond cross-entropy: what else can an LM loss be?) [WebFetch to kexue.fm failed twice; read from the Wayback snapshot of 2026-08-09]
posts.core_insight: Training targets arrive one sample at a time, so a usable loss must be linear in the target distribution, L(p,q)=E_{i~p}[S(q,i)], and minimised at q=p. That forces S to be the tangent plane of a concave 'entropy' H: S(q,i)=H(q)+(e_i−q)·∇H(q). These are the proper scoring rules (log/cross-entropy, Brier, Tsallis, spherical, Rényi); if S may depend only on q_i, cross-entropy is the only option. With softmax logits z, the cross-entropy gradient is q−e_i: it is convex and vanishes only when the prediction is correct. Brier's gradient is 2(diag q−qqᵀ)(q−e_i), which also vanishes when the model is confidently wrong: it learns slowly early but is robust to noisy or hard labels late, so Su suggests cross-entropy as the main loss and Brier-type losses late. Conversely, every H has a matched activation q=∇Φ(z), with Φ(z)=max_p p·z+H(p) (Fenchel-Young losses: softmax for Shannon entropy, sparsemax/entmax for Tsallis), which restores the clean q−e_i gradient.
posts.rl_transfer: (1) Train the critic as a proper-score classifier. With a2r's sparse +1/−0.25 reward the value is essentially a success probability, so use a Bernoulli-logit or HL-Gauss/two-hot head with log loss instead of the MSE v_loss in _task_backward. a2r already normalises returns per task (value_norm), so the gain is not scale balancing but clean gradients and calibrated log-odds on rare successes, such as upstream pregrasp/reach starts near 0%. This is close to Farebrother et al. 2024 ('Stop Regressing'), so it is an ingredient, not a headline. (2) For teacher→RGB-D student DAgger (the bc term at origin/main policy.py:300-309), use the log score (NLL) early and a bounded score (spherical or Gaussian-kernel) late, so states where the teacher itself is wrong stop dominating; this is Su's 'cross-entropy early, Brier late' rule. (3) Diagnosis for the std-floor finding (noisy success rises while the deterministic mean lags): an advantage-weighted Gaussian fit is a log-score, moment-matching fit, so it averages distinct success modes such as releasing at different steps. A redescending score pulls μ onto one mode instead; see the concrete version under DiVeQ.

posts.title: 直接以FID为Loss：从梯度计算到流式训练 (FID directly as a loss: from gradients to streaming training) [WebFetch failed twice and no archive copy exists; read through the r.jina.ai reader]
posts.core_insight: The Fréchet distance between Gaussian fits of encoder features is ‖μp−μq‖²+tr(Σp+Σq−2(Σp^{1/2}ΣqΣp^{1/2})^{1/2}). It is differentiable, with ∇_{Σq}=I−Σp^{1/2}(Σp^{1/2}ΣqΣp^{1/2})^{−1/2}Σp^{1/2}, but it is a nonlinear function of batch-level statistics: small batches give biased, rank-deficient estimates, and plain gradient accumulation does not remove the bias. The exact fix computes the big-batch moments over k micro-batches, then backpropagates each micro-batch through F(sg[μ−μ̃_i/k]+μ̃_i/k, sg[V−Ṽ_i/k]+Ṽ_i/k), so the summed gradients equal the big-batch gradient. The streaming fix ('history makes up the batch') keeps EMA moments and stop-gradients the history, F_t=F(β·sg[μ_{t−1}]+(1−β)μ̃_t, β·sg[V_{t−1}]+(1−β)Ṽ_t), and works better than a queue of past batches. Losses from several encoders are balanced by self-normalising each one, L=Σ_i F_i/(sg[F_i]+ε).
posts.rl_transfer: Advantage normalisation is the same kind of batch-level nonlinear statistic. a2r divides each task's advantages by that task's batch std at every update (origin/main a2r/benchmark/contact_rl/policy.py:274) and averages the task losses with equal weight; our wrwl/ppo.py:653-654 normalises per minibatch. When a task or start type has no successes, that std is just critic noise, so the division inflates noise to unit size. Our 10-31 notes record pre-success PPO random-walking on critic noise and eroding learned skills. The lab's comment at policy.py:193-197 records noisy per-task KLs pinning the max-KL adaptive rate: the ten-task joint run ended near lr 3e-5, against 4e-4 to 1e-3 for single tasks. The transfer is to normalise with per-task EMA moments carried across iterations (β≈0.95-0.99) and floored at about 0.05-0.1 of the success reward. A zero-signal task's update and KL then stay small until real signal arrives, while tasks with signal are normalised as before. Two options: give each task its own KL-adaptive loss coefficient instead of one global KL-driven rate, and balance per-task BC/DAgger losses with Σ_k L_k/(sg[L_k]+ε). This targets joint multi-task interference at its source rather than through the max→mean symptom fix, along with the pre-success erosion and plausibly the wiping that follows when the unlock curriculum adds 0% start types. No reset or SGS change.

posts.title: 生成扩散模型漫谈（三十一）：预测数据而非噪声 (Predict data, not noise: JiT) [read from Wayback snapshot]
posts.core_insight: Noise has full-dimensional support, and so does velocity, which contains noise; clean data lies on a low-dimensional manifold. A network with a low-rank bottleneck (for example 32×32×3 = 3072-dim patches projected to 768) therefore cannot fit noise targets, so ε- and v-prediction fail while x-prediction still trains. JiT keeps whatever regression loss is used but parameterises v=(NN(x_t,t)−x_t)/(1−t): the network predicts the clean sample, and the −x_t skip connection carries the full-rank part. The prediction target matters far more than the loss target, and a modest bottleneck even helps x-prediction, which makes moving from low to high resolution cheap.
posts.rl_transfer: This applies only to flow/diffusion action heads: an RGB-D student or VLA with action chunks (e.g., 16 steps × 7 dof = 112 outputs from a 256/512-wide head), or a future flow-head RL policy. Predict the clean action chunk with the skip parameterisation rather than velocity or noise; this keeps narrow heads trainable and fits our measurement that the policy occupies about 20 of 256 hidden dimensions. The current Gaussian PPO teacher has no clean analogue: its mean is 7-dimensional, so there is no output bottleneck.

posts.title: 生成扩散模型漫谈（三十）：从瞬时速度到平均速度 (From instantaneous to average velocity: MeanFlow) [read from Wayback snapshot]
posts.core_insight: MeanFlow models the average velocity over an interval, u(x_t,r,t)=(1/(t−r))∫_r^t v dτ, instead of the ODE's instantaneous velocity, so the one-step update x_0=x_1−u(x_1,0,1) is exact rather than an Euler approximation. Differentiating (t−r)u gives the identity v=u+(t−r)·du/dt, where du/dt=v·∂_x u+∂_t u is a Jacobian-vector product. Substituting this into flow matching gives ‖u_θ+(t−r)·sg[JVP]−(x_1−x_0)‖², which at r=t reduces to ordinary flow matching, a built-in safety net. Su shows that putting u(x_t,t,t) inside the JVP gives a single explicit minimisation with no EMA or stop-gradient (adding the stop-gradient only roughly halves training time). MeanFlow's own choice, x_1−x_0 inside the JVP, ties the objective to the optimiser, as in consistency models.
posts.rl_transfer: For flow action heads: a one-step MeanFlow head makes a multimodal policy as cheap as a Gaussian at inference. The RGB-D student can then be trained on the stochastic teacher's successful actions, covering all success modes, and deployed in one step. Noisy successes are consolidated in the student, which is deployed anyway, instead of waiting for the teacher's mean to become reliable (the slow phase we see with std floors). The r=t fallback is also a design rule for any loss we add: keep the base PPO/BC objective as a special case that is always trained, e.g., 75% of samples on the base objective and 25% on the new one. No change for the Gaussian PPO teacher itself.

posts.title: 生成扩散模型漫谈（二十八）：分步理解一致性模型 (Consistency models, step by step) [read from Wayback snapshot]
posts.core_insight: Decompose flow-matching denoising into steps: at t_k, regress f_θ(x_{t_k},t_k) onto the previous step's solution f_{θ*_{k−1}}(x_{t_{k−1}},t_{k−1}) rather than onto x_0, because a nearer target is easier and reduces trajectory crossing (one input with many targets). Sharing one network across steps puts the unknown optimum into the target, so it is replaced by an 'ahead' solution, the EMA weights θ̄, giving the loss ‖f_θ(x_{t_k},t_k)−f_θ̄(x_{t_{k−1}},t_{k−1})‖². Summed over k, this telescopes into an upper bound on ‖f(x_1,1)−x_0‖, which is what allows one-step generation. Consistency distillation takes x_{t_{k−1}} from one step of the teacher's solver.
posts.rl_transfer: Use an EMA 'ahead' policy. Keep θ̄=EMA(θ) of the actor (β≈0.99 per optimiser step), run the deterministic 1024-2048-episode evals and deployment on μ_θ̄, and optionally add ‖μ_θ(s)−sg[μ_θ̄(s)]‖² on rollout states. It costs nothing and should be the first control against the finding that the deterministic mean lags or collapses first while noisy training success rises. The 'nearer target' chain maps onto staged starts (pregrasp→reach→grasp→insert) as bootstrapping from the next stage's EMA critic, but GAE already bootstraps, so expect little gain for upstream starts stuck near 0%.

posts.title: 生成扩散模型漫谈（二十七）：将步长作为条件输入 (Step size as a conditioning input: Shortcut models) [read from Wayback snapshot]
posts.core_insight: Shortcut models make the velocity a function of the step size, x_{t+ε}=x_t+v(x_t,t,ε)ε. They train ε=0 with flow matching and add a self-consistency loss saying one step of 2ε equals two steps of ε: v(x_t,t,2ε)≈sg[(v(x_t,t,ε)+v(x̃_{t+ε},t+ε,ε))/2], with x̃_{t+ε}=x_t+v(x_t,t,ε)ε. Step sizes 2^−7 to 1 enter as an embedding; 3/4 of each batch trains the flow loss and 1/4 the consistency loss, which gives one-step generation from a single training stage. Su relates it to CTM and to AMED's mean-value-theorem solver.
posts.rl_transfer: For our purposes MeanFlow subsumes this as the one-step flow head. The only control-specific analogue is a policy conditioned on its control interval, trained with a(s,2k)≈sg[(a(s,k)+a(s′,k))/2] using the simulator's next state. That amounts to learned action repeat (coarse steps for free-space reach, fine steps in contact); it is low priority and not tied to any measured pain point.

posts.title: 生成扩散模型漫谈（二十六）：基于恒等式的蒸馏（下） (Identity-based distillation, part 2: SiD and FGM) [read from Wayback snapshot]
posts.core_insight: SiD trains a one-step generator θ so that the teacher's denoiser ε_φ* matches a 'fake' denoiser ψ*(θ) fitted to generator samples. In practice ψ* is treated as a constant, which biases the gradient. FGM uses the identity E⟨f(x_t),ε_ψ*(x_t)⟩=E⟨f(x_t),ε⟩, valid only when f depends on x_t alone, to build L4=2L2^(sg)−L1^(sg), whose stop-gradient version has exactly the true gradient; this explains SiD's λ=0.5. Su adds that the generator distribution appears twice in the Fisher divergence: as the sampling measure and inside the score. Gradients through the sampling measure only invite mode collapse, because the generator can move its samples to where the mismatch is small, so that occurrence should be stop-gradiented. This gives the practical loss 2(L2−L1), i.e. λ=1; λ slightly above 1 acts as an anti-collapse penalty, and λ=1.5 already diverges.
posts.rl_transfer: The 'two occurrences' rule applies to every regulariser on on-policy states, E_{s~d^π}[ℓ(π(·|s),π_ref(·|s))]: keep d^π stop-gradiented as a per-state loss term, as our --prior_ckpt reverse KL and a2r's bc term already do. Never put anchors, imitation or consolidation terms into the reward. There the policy gradient would let the policy lower the penalty by avoiding states where it must differ from the reference, such as the release seam in Pick→Place. This applies directly to the new terms proposed under DiVeQ. For a future flow/diffusion teacher, SiD/FGM also give data-free one-step distillation into the student. It is a design rule more than a new recipe.

posts.title: DiVeQ：一种非常简洁的VQ训练方案 (DiVeQ: a very simple VQ training scheme) [read from Wayback snapshot]
posts.core_insight: DiVeQ replaces VQ's straight-through estimator z_q=z+sg[q−z] with z_q=z+‖q−z‖·sg[(q−z)/‖q−z‖]. The forward value is still exactly the code q, but gradients also flow through the distance. This is equivalent to an automatically weighted auxiliary loss, sg[⟨∇_{z_q}L,q−z⟩]·ln‖q−z‖ ≈ sg[L(z_q)−L(z)]·α·ln‖q−z‖. The coefficient is the loss gap between the deployed (quantised) path and the trainable (continuous) path: it is positive once training works, scales with the main loss and fades as the gap closes, so no auxiliary-loss weights need tuning. Adding a little noise to the direction (σ²=1e-3) interpolates toward NSVQ (random direction, with a train/test mismatch); Su prefers the noiseless detach version with α=1.
posts.rl_transfer: This is a template for the std-floor finding: noisy training success rises fast, the deterministic mean lags, and turning noisy successes into a reliable mean is the slow part. Treat μ+σε as the trainable path and μ as the deployed path, and add L_cons=sg[(SR_σ−SR_0)_+]·E_{(s,a)∈successful noisy episodes} ln(‖μ_θ(s)−a‖²/σ²+δ). Here SR_σ is training success, and SR_0 is measured every iteration on a small deterministic slice of envs (e.g., 64 of 2048), excluded from PPO like a2r's teacher_exec samples. The gap coefficient turns the term on only while noisy successes outnumber deterministic ones and off once the mean catches up, so it cannot hurt when the source already succeeds. The log-distance form is a Cauchy-type redescending pull, so μ locks onto the dominant success mode instead of averaging modes. It also moves the gripper mean across the release threshold that the noise was already crossing. The same gap signal can drive the exploration floor, and a per-stage version, sg[SR_stage,best−SR_stage,now]_+, can gate an anti-forgetting KL for stages the unlock curriculum wipes. It fits a2r's existing bc_weight path (policy.py:300-309) with self-generated labels, as a per-state loss, never a reward. No reset or SGS change.

posts.title: VQ的又一技巧：给编码表加一个线性变换 (Another VQ trick: a linear map on the codebook, SimVQ) [read from Wayback snapshot]
posts.core_insight: SimVQ reparameterises the codebook as e_i=q_iW with one shared linear map W (the q_i can even stay at their random initialisation). The function class is unchanged, but the optimiser dynamics change: W is updated from every selected code's gradient, so even unselected codes move, Δe_i≈−η(∂L/∂e_i·WᵀW+q_iΣ_j q_jᵀ∂L/∂e_j). This removes dead codes, speeds convergence and raises codebook utilisation; a diagonal W recovers part of the gain. Su frames it as overparameterisation, like the RMSNorm gain that could be merged into the next layer, and suggests a shared linear map after all MoE experts for the same reason.
posts.rl_transfer: Two cheap, speculative knobs. (a) For reuse: insert identity-initialised linear layers after the source trunk's hidden layers. The function is unchanged and the layers can be merged back for deployment, but the extra overparameterisation may speed fine-tuning; this is consistent with our results that full fine-tuning with the floor is fastest and that training subsets of units is slower. (b) Per-task parameters that are rarely updated, such as embeddings for tasks or start types the curriculum seldom samples, behave like dead codes; parameterising them through a shared W lets them move. Do not share per-task log-std this way: a2r's own code comment notes that a shared std lets tasks that already succeed shrink the noise of tasks still searching for a first success. Each knob takes minutes to test in ManiSkill.

posts.title: 生成扩散模型漫谈（二十九）：用DDPM来离散编码 (Discrete encoding with DDPM: DDCM) [read from Wayback snapshot]
posts.core_insight: DDCM restricts DDPM's per-step noise to a fixed codebook C_t of K pre-sampled Gaussian vectors, independent for each step. FID is nearly unchanged at K=64 and degrades little even at K=2; a single codebook shared across steps needs K≥8192. Encoding a given x_0 becomes guided generation: at each step pick ε_t=argmax_{ε∈C_t} ε·(x_0−x̂_0(x_t)), the code best aligned with the gap between the target and the current clean-sample prediction. The principled version samples ε by softmax with logits −½‖ε−c_t(x_0−x̂_0(x_t))‖², so that K→∞ recovers DDPM; the same rule gives classifier guidance with ∇log p(y|x_t).
posts.rl_transfer: Little for our setting. The analogue is guided exploration noise: draw K candidate ε per step and choose by softmax over ε·g(s) for a guidance direction g, such as ∇_a of a success classifier. As K→∞ this just shifts the exploration mean by κg (as in optimistic actor-critic), and it complicates PPO's likelihood ratio. Bit-reproducible GPU sims would allow storing noise seeds instead of trajectories, but storing (s,a) is simpler.

posts.title: 细水长flow之TARFLOW：流模型满血归来？ (TARFLOW: normalising flows are back?) [read from Wayback snapshot]
posts.core_insight: TARFLOW brings normalising flows close to state of the art by stacking Transformer autoregressive affine couplings over spatial patches, h_k=exp(γ_k(x_{<k}))⊙x_k+β_k(x_{<k}), which gives the exact likelihood −log N(f(x))−Σγ. Training adds Gaussian noise to the data, and sampling removes it with the model's own score (Tweedie's formula), x=y+σ²∇_y log q_θ(y), so no separate denoiser is needed. Sampling is slow because the inverse is a nonlinear RNN; invertibility also allows backprop without storing activations.
posts.rl_transfer: (a) A small autoregressive flow head over the 7 action dims, with the gripper conditioned on the arm dims, gives PPO exact log-probabilities for multimodal actions. Deploying z=0 picks a mode of the learned distribution, rather than a Gaussian mean that may average success modes. (b) The noise-then-Tweedie view explains the std floor. With a=μ+σε, PPO's mean follows the gradient of the Gaussian-smoothed objective J_σ(μ)=E_ε[R(μ+σε)] (Stein's identity: ∇J_σ=E[Rε]/σ). A floor lets rare successes ignite learning. But for a threshold event such as a gripper release, J_σ=Φ((μ−τ)/σ) has slope φ(·)/σ, which is flat when σ is large, so the mean crosses the threshold slowly while the noise already crosses it: that is the deterministic lag. For non-convex success sets, the maximiser of J_σ can also fall outside the set. To test the diagnosis, compare μ against a Tweedie-shifted μ′=μ+σ²∇_a log p_succ(a|s)|_{a=μ}, using a small density model fitted to successful actions.

best_ideas: 1. Gap-gated consolidation of noisy successes (from DiVeQ, with the mode-seeking form motivated by the scoring-rule and TARFLOW posts). Problem: with an exploration floor, training success rises but the deterministic mean lags or collapses, and that consolidation is the slow part. Recipe: run about 3% of envs deterministically, excluded from the PPO loss, to measure SR_0 every iteration, and add the per-state loss L_cons=sg[(SR_σ−SR_0)_+]·E_{successful noisy (s,a)} ln(‖μ_θ(s)−a‖²/σ²+δ) (never as a reward). Spend day 1 on diagnosis: on ManiSkill Stack/Place/PushRetreat checkpoints where SR_σ≫SR_0, compare μ, the EMA-weight policy (from the consistency-model post), the mean of successful actions and a Tweedie-shifted μ, to tell threshold crossing at gripper release apart from mode averaging. Then measure time-to-90% deterministic success over 3 seeds against reuse+floor, constant-weight self-imitation, a plain MSE pull and floor annealing, and port to a2r insert_key insert→insert+turn. Kill it if it is not at least 1.3× faster on 2 of 3 pairs. Prior-art risk: self-imitation learning (Oh 2018). The new parts are the self-tuning deployed-minus-trained gap coefficient and the redescending pull.

2. Signal-calibrated advantage scaling for multi-task and multi-start PPO (from the FID-loss post's EMA statistics, 'history makes up the batch'). Mechanism to test: per-task std normalisation (a2r origin/main policy.py:274) or per-minibatch normalisation (wrwl/ppo.py:653) inflates critic noise to unit size whenever a task or start type has no successes. That plausibly drives three problems: the pre-success skill erosion recorded on 10-31, the noisy per-task KLs that pinned a2r's max-KL learning rate (ten-task joint lr about 3e-5), and the wiping when the curriculum unlocks 0% starts. Recipe: per-task EMA moments of the advantages across iterations (β≈0.95-0.99), floored at 0.05-0.1 times the success reward, so zero-signal tasks make small updates with small KLs; optionally, per-task KL-adaptive loss coefficients instead of one global rate. Cheap falsification first: log each task's share of the gradient norm and its KL while at 0% success (SGS may already starve such cells of envs). Then test in three settings: (i) ManiSkill reuse runs, measuring source-skill erosion and time-to-90%; (ii) a 3-task a2r joint run with one 0% task under the original max-KL rule, to see whether the solo-vs-joint gap closes without the max→mean fix; (iii) stage retention across an unlock event. It is a one-line change with no reset or SGS change. Nearest prior art is Dr. GRPO's removal of std normalisation in LLM RL.

3. Gap-driven exploration floor (the DiVeQ gap signal plus the Tweedie view from TARFLOW). Our ManiSkill runs show the floor pays off only when the source almost never succeeds on the target, and slows learning 2-3× when the source already succeeds. Set σ_floor,t=σ_max·(1−SR_0,t)^κ from the same deterministic slice as idea 1. The floor stays full while the deterministic policy fails; ignition is unaffected because SR_0 stays low while noisy successes snowball. It fades as the mean becomes reliable, and starts small when the source already succeeds. Combined with idea 1, this gives a self-tuning 'ignite, then consolidate' recipe with no hand-set anneal. Test on PushRetreat (source at about 0%) against Place/Stack (source partly succeeds) and against a2r's global 0.6 gripper floor, reporting time-to-90%. Pass criterion: match the best fixed floor on PushRetreat and beat it on Place/Stack.

4. Consolidate in the deployed student, not the teacher (MeanFlow plus JiT). a2r deploys an RGB-D student distilled from the RL teacher, so train the student's one-step MeanFlow head, with clean-action (x-pred) parameterisation, on the stochastic teacher's successful actions plus DAgger relabels. The student captures every success mode and runs in one step, so teacher training can stop once noisy success is high instead of waiting for the teacher's mean to reach 90%. Keep the r=t flow-matching fallback in every batch and keep the student's state distribution stop-gradiented, as the SiD post argues. This is heavier because it needs the student pipeline, so it is material for the full paper (Apr 2027) rather than the Dec 4 extended abstract.

posts.title: 简单谈谈K3的MoE和Attention (A brief look at K3's MoE and attention)
posts.core_insight: K3 = KDA + MLA + Stable LatentMoE + AttnRes, trained with Moonlight-style Muon applied per attention head; the MoE changes are stability fixes. SwiGLU blows up when a row of W1 and a row of W2 both align with the same input (an O(|x|^4) outlier), so K3 bounds both branches: output = W3( SiTU(W1x; 4) ⊙ softcap(W2x; 25) ), with softcap(x;β) = β·tanh(x/β) and SiTU = softcap(x)·sigmoid(x); a softcap beats a hard clip at the same bound. LatentMoE (d→d/2→2n-choose-2k experts→d/2→d) is a product of four matrices and unstable; one RMSNorm just before the d/2→d up-projection is the essential fix, and it also rebalances routed vs shared experts so no scale factor is needed. Quantile balancing reads global quantiles from 1000-bin histograms, which add across GPUs and gradient-accumulation steps.
posts.rl_transfer: Hygiene for the trunk-reuse experiments rather than a recipe. (1) If we add a low-rank adapter or new head onto a reused source trunk for stage extension (d→r→d), put an RMSNorm right before the r→d re-expansion and softcap any multiplicative branch (task-embedding FiLM or gates × point-cloud features) instead of hard-clipping; that is the same 'product of matrices' instability. (2) Use EMA'd, mergeable histogram quantiles (100–1000 bins) for per-task robust statistics inside PPO, such as return/advantage scale and success thresholds; they are causal, cheap over 1–2k envs and add across our two GPUs. (3) If we ever use Muon or other orthogonalised updates for the actor, orthogonalise each output group separately (arm rows, gripper rows, each task's head) so the large arm gradient cannot wash out the small release gradient. None of these addresses a core pain point on its own.

posts.title: MoE环游记：9、门控归一化之争 (MoE journey 9: the gate-normalisation debate)
posts.core_insight: The router score plays two roles: Router (which experts run) and Gate (multiplied into the expert so the router gets gradients). Start from the principle 'argmax of the router = argmin over experts of the loss'. Minimising KL(p‖q) with q_i ∝ exp(−loss(e_i)/τ) leaves the effective loss Σ p_i·loss(e_i), whose gradient E_{i∼p}[∇log p_i · loss(e_i)] is REINFORCE. Subtracting the baseline loss(0) and Taylor-expanding to first order gives a straight-through estimator; scaling each expert by its own probability (p_i·e_i) makes forward and backward consistent: E[∇log p_i·(loss(p_i e_i) − loss(0))] ≈ ∇E[loss(p_i e_i)]. Hence gates should be normalised but not re-normalised after top-k (with k=1, re-norm gives the router zero gradient), and top-k vs sampling is a stability vs diversity trade-off, bridged by 'take top-(k+c), then pick k at random' or small logit noise.
posts.rl_transfer: This post bridges likelihood-ratio and reparameterised gradients, which is exactly our slowest phase. Under a std floor, training success rises while the deterministic mean lags or collapses (ManiSkill), and a2r shows the same gap: sweep pregrasp training EMA is about 0.90 against about 0.53 in frozen deterministic eval (E-10 O-219, which leaves it unexplained). With a large floor, PPO optimises the Gaussian-smoothed return. The gradient of that return toward a narrow success region shrinks roughly like w/σ², and its maximiser need not be the best deterministic action. Applying Su's baseline-plus-Taylor step to a Gaussian policy, with a privileged action-value head Q(s,a) added to the existing privileged critic, gives a Q-Prop-style actor loss: run PPO on the residual advantage A − ⟨∇aQ(s,μ), a−μ⟩, and add an analytic term −η·Q(s, μθ(s)). That term trains the deterministic mean directly and does not decay with σ. A cheaper variant regresses μθ onto the noisy actions of successful rollouts, using the 11626 gate. A second transfer: model release/close as a categorical open/close/hold head whose probability gates the gripper-rate command (deterministic = argmax), and explore with a bounded flip floor (the top-(k+c)-random-k analogue) instead of a Gaussian std floor that wastes variance on magnitudes. a2r's release needs 6–11 consecutive positive rate steps, which i.i.d. Gaussian noise rarely produces. Third: any per-task or per-skill experts in the teacher or student should use softmax gates multiplied into the experts, with no re-norm. Q-Prop, IPG and SIL are prior art, so novelty must come from the floor-then-consolidate recipe, not from the estimator.

posts.title: MoE环游记：8、强制序列级均衡 (MoE journey 8: enforcing sequence-level balance)
posts.core_insight: Loss-Free biases are global, so they balance only the batch. To balance within each sequence, causally and without an aux loss, Moving Quantile Balancing gives each position its own bias β_i = the (1 − k/n) quantile of recent router scores. Quantiles cannot be updated incrementally, so scores in [0,1] are one-hot bucketed into b bins, the histograms are EMA'd along the sequence (γ = 0.99, b = 100), and β_i is read from the EMA CDF. Routing uses s_i − β_i, plus a global QB step for top-k, while the gate keeps the raw scores. On a 3B 128-choose-4 MoE, full sequence balance (λ = 1) costs 0.06 loss, while partial balance s_i − λβ_i with λ ≈ 0.3 is lossless and still balances better: perfect uniformity hurts.
posts.rl_transfer: (1) The EMA-histogram quantile is a causal, linear, mergeable estimator for per-task or per-start-type statistics in PPO. Use it for a signal-aware advantage scale: divide each task's advantages by max(S_t, S_min), where S_t is an EMA-histogram P95−P5 range of that task's returns (DreamerV3 does this with max(1, S)), instead of per-task std normalisation. a2r's joint learner normalises advantages per task, and so did our ManiSkill PPO. That forces unit-size updates even from tasks or start types with no success yet, and our own diagnosis is that pre-success PPO random-walks on critic noise and erodes unanchored skills. (2) The λ lesson applies to any equalisation across tasks. a2r's max-KL rule, its mean-KL fix and full per-task KL equalisation are points on one continuum, and Su's data predict that a partial setting (λ ≈ 0.3–0.5) is best. Per-episode ('sequence-level') balancing of exploration is not worth pursuing, since our data show local exploration does not beat global.

posts.title: DeepSeek V4的tid2eid是怎么来的？ (Where does DeepSeek V4's tid2eid table come from?)
posts.core_insight: DSV4 swaps 'first_k_dense' for 'first_k_hash': the first MoE layers route each token through a fixed token-id→expert table, because early layers carry little context. Building the table is min Σ_j (Σ_i p_i x_ij − k/n)² subject to each token picking k experts, where p_i is token frequency. A greedy pass in descending frequency that hands each token the k currently least-loaded experts is near-optimal. If one token's frequency exceeds k/n, no 1-gram table can balance, so n-grams are hashed instead ((a·q + b) mod n). Readers report that randomising half of DSV4-Flash's table without retraining moves benchmarks by under 1%, and that greedy tables lock experts into fixed groups (fixed by sampling in proportion to remaining load budget).
posts.rl_transfer: Little to take for a training recipe. The RL analogue is fixed task- or start-type-indexed parameter blocks in the first trunk layers, balanced by sample share. That is hard parameter isolation, and our evidence argues against it: training a key or random subset of units is slower than full fine-tuning (key == random), old and new tasks share a ~20-dim subspace, and a2r's joint shortfalls were traced to LR rules, std collapse and curricula. The reader result that a random routing table is almost as good as a designed one mirrors our key == random finding: the identity of a fixed partition barely matters. That argues for spending effort on optimiser and exploration allocation rather than on routing. The greedy least-loaded assignment could balance task→GPU or env-process placement, but that is infrastructure.

posts.title: MoE环游记：7、动态激活极简解 (MoE journey 7: a minimal solution for dynamic activation)
posts.core_insight: Drop the per-token 'exactly k experts' constraint and keep only the per-expert load Σ_i x_ij = mk/n. The LP dual then gives activation x_ij = 1 iff s_ij > β_j, and the dual objective Σ_ij max(0, s_ij − β_j) + (mk/n)Σ_j β_j is minimised exactly, in one step, by β_j = the (1 − k/n) quantile of expert j's scores: no iteration and no learning rate. In training, route with the old β, then update β ← 0.9β + 0.1·quantile; the EMA avoids overfitting one batch and the order avoids leakage. Initialise β0 = σ·Φ⁻¹(1 − k/n) from the initial logit scale σ ≈ σ̃√d. One SignSGD step on the dual gradient (mk/n − #active) recovers the earlier dynamic Loss-Free rule.
posts.rl_transfer: A general budgeted gate for RL recipes. When an intervention should fire on a fixed fraction q of samples per task, set that task's threshold to the EMA'd (1−q) quantile of the score, computed on the previous batch and applied to the current one. No per-task coefficient tuning is needed across tasks with different success rates or reward scales. Main use, for the consolidation bottleneck, is quantile-gated self-imitation: add a regression of the mean μθ(s) onto the executed noisy action for each task's top-q advantage samples (q ≈ 5–10%, restricted to successful episodes while successes are rare), weighted so every task gets the same budget. Under the floor, PPO's mean signal is the Gaussian-smoothed gradient; the regression pulls the mean directly onto the actions that worked. Secondary uses: a quantile/Φ⁻¹ initialisation for exploration floors instead of hand-picked 0.3 or 0.6, and a budgeted gate for extra distillation weight on 拐点 frames (gripper or contact switches) in the teacher→student DAgger stage. It touches neither resets nor SGS. Prior art is SIL and AWR/CRR filtered BC; the per-task budget gate is the new part.

posts.title: MoE环游记：6、最优分配促均衡 (MoE journey 6: optimal allocation for load balance)
posts.core_insight: Load balancing becomes the assignment LP: maximise Σ x_ij s_ij subject to Σ_j x_ij = k per token and Σ_i x_ij = mk/n per expert. The [0,1] relaxation is tight. After swapping max and min, the primal is x_ij = 1 iff s_ij − α_i − β_j > 0, with closed-form alternating duals α_i = the (k+1)-th largest of s_i − β and β_j = the (mk/n+1)-th largest of s_:,j − α; both are (1 − k/n) quantiles, hence Quantile Balancing (QB). Only β is needed at inference. In training, warm-start from last step's β, do one iteration, route with the old β first, and average micro-batch quantiles. QB has no step-size hyperparameter and balances even the first MoE layer, where SignSGD Loss-Free fails. The inequality-constrained BIP variant clips the duals at 0 and only 'robs the rich' without 'helping the poor'.
posts.rl_transfer: This maps onto how a2r's joint learner shares one trust region across tasks. The KL-adaptive LR is a single dual variable for ten tasks, and driving it with the max per-task KL is BIP-like: it only throttles. In 10-task runs the LR fell to 2e-5–8e-5, against 4.4e-4–1e-3 single-task. The mean rule (R212, 150 min) brought nine tasks to 80–100%, but sweep stayed at 36.6/33.5% (97.9% alone, with ~60% of eval episodes timing out) and egg at 12.9/14.8%. Sweep only reached 94% in R217, with reverse curricula and 720 min, and deposit_coin and egg remain weak. QB-style recipe: give each task (optionally each start-type group) a loss weight w_t that is a non-gradient dual. Solve it in closed form after each PPO epoch from the measured KL: since KL_t ≈ c_t·w_t², set w_t ← w_t·(δ/KL_t)^(λ/2) with EMA 0.9 and λ ≈ 0.5, normalised to mean 1. Apply the previous weights first, and let the global LR track mean KL with a proportional log-space rule instead of ×1.5 jumps. Each task then moves at about its single-task step size inside one shared update, so starved tasks are boosted, not only hot ones throttled. Pair it with the signal-aware advantage scale (11760) so zero-success tasks are not pushed to full KL on noise. Caveat: first rule out a budget confound, since R212's sweep got roughly 10× fewer env-steps than the single-task run (256 vs 1024 envs, ~600 vs 1381 updates). Test on ManiSkill 4-task joint PPO, then a 3–4-task a2r joint run on one 4090; the metric is per-task env-steps-to-90%, joint vs single.

posts.title: MoE环游记：5、均匀分布的反思 (MoE journey 5: rethinking the uniform distribution)
posts.core_insight: Shared experts (s always-on experts plus (k−s)-of-(n−s) routed ones) help at no extra cost. The shared part absorbs what all experts have in common, so the routed experts learn residuals that are closer to orthogonal. In y = Σ_shared e_i + λ·Σ_routed ρ_i e_i, λ should make both branches equally large at initialisation: λ ≈ √s / √(Σ ρ_i²) for unit-norm orthogonal experts and N(0,1) logits, and simulation reproduces DeepSeek-V2's 16 and V3's 2.5. Shared experts also show that uniform load is not optimal, since real data are Zipf-like: keep routed experts uniform for parallelism and let shared ones carry the non-uniform mass. Finer-grained experts (C(2n,2k) ≫ C(n,k)) cover non-uniform knowledge better.
posts.rl_transfer: Applies to warm starts and stage extension. a2r warm starts from single-task checkpoints failed for tasks missing from the checkpoint, which 'inherit a mode they cannot leave'. E10-R214 left hang and stack at 0 after 250 updates even with gripper floor 0.6; E10-R216 left sweep at 0%, stalling to timeout, and other tasks below scratch. Joint init only speeds hard start types ~2× with no zero-shot transfer (O-222). In ManiSkill the new task lies 94–97% inside the old ~20-dim subspace, and full FT + floor was fastest. Recipe to test: keep the reused trunk as the 'shared expert', fully fine-tuned, and add a small task- or stage-routed residual branch (rank 8–32, RMSNorm before the up-projection per 11848). Set its output scale λ by Su's norm-matching rule at init: zero-init would reproduce the inherited mode and random re-init would lose reuse. Compare against full FT + floor on Pick→Stack, insert_key insert→insert+turn and an R214-style warm start. The 'uniform is not optimal' point also means any per-task equalisation (as in 11619) should keep a shared, non-equalised component.

posts.title: MoE环游记：4、难处应当多投入 (MoE journey 4: harder tokens deserve more compute)
posts.core_insight: Make the number of active experts dynamic by routing with argwhere(ρ + b > 0) instead of top-k. The bias has a redundant degree of freedom, since adding a constant does not change top-k, so its centred part can enforce balance while its mean controls the average budget k: b ← b − γ[sign(F − Q) − mean(sign(F − Q)) + sign(|F̃| − k)]. The simpler b ← b − γ·sign(F̃ − k/n) works too but jitters more early. Replacing sign with RMS normalisation, (F̃ − Q̃)/RMS(F̃ − Q̃), keeps the step scale while small errors give small steps, which is slightly smoother. b can be initialised by bisection on simulated initial scores.
posts.rl_transfer: Two concrete pieces. (1) The RMS-normalised, proportional dual update is a drop-in replacement for a2r's KL-adaptive LR, which multiplies or divides by 1.5 whenever KL leaves [0.5×, 2×] the target. That is a bang-bang sign rule, and with noisy small-minibatch KL it ratchets down; the docs note the LR pinned at 1e-5 with 256 envs. Use log lr ← log lr − γ·(log KL − log δ), clipped. (2) The redundant-DOF split gives a clean way to parameterise exploration across tasks: a global log-std offset sets the total exploration budget and a centred per-task part sets the allocation, each with its own controller. That replaces hand-set per-interaction floors (hang 0.3, egg needs 0.6, 1.0 learns too slowly) and scales to a2r's planned 50 tasks. The headline 'hard inputs get more' (more noise or compute on hard states) has weak support for exploration, since our local-vs-global test was a tie. Use it only for distillation compute, e.g. extra loss weight or an extra expert on 拐点 frames budgeted by the 11626 quantile gate.

posts.title: MoE环游记：3、换个思路来分配 (MoE journey 3: a different way to allocate)
posts.core_insight: DeepSeek's Loss-Free balancing changes the assignment, not the scores. Route with argtop_k(ρ + b) but gate with ρ, and update the input-independent bias by b ← b − γ·sign(F − Q), where F is the current load and Q uniform. Su derives this as an STE aux loss ½‖b + sg[F − b] − Q‖², whose gradient is F − Q, and finds that RMS-normalised steps (F − Q)/RMS(F − Q) balance better at the same γ. He names the real innovation: one bias vector is enough to enforce balance, so the auxiliary objective updates only b while the LM loss updates everything else, and the two never compete for shared parameters. Rules: update b after the model step (no leakage); decouple the bias activation (sigmoid, so γ = 1e-3 transfers) from the gate activation; the same trick solves assignment problems and VQ codebook collapse.
posts.rl_transfer: The isolation principle is the most useful single idea in the set. Our RL stack bolts auxiliary objectives onto shared parameters: entropy bonus (0.003 in a2r), gripper bias/std init, std floors, KL anchors to the source, BC terms. Loss-Free says: find the one low-dimensional knob that is enough for the constraint and update it outside the gradient, with a sign or proportional rule, after the policy step. Concretely, replace the entropy bonus and the hand-tuned per-interaction floors with a per-task log-std floor φ_t that is a controlled variable, not a hyperparameter. Before ignition, steer φ_t toward a monotone exploration target: a per-dimension entropy target, or for gripper seams the fraction of episodes with at least one release event. After training success appears, steer it toward closing the stochastic–deterministic success gap, so the floor removes itself. Decide with the old φ, update after the rollout, and take RMS-normalised steps. This addresses std collapse before release is found (hang_mugs, fill_egg_holder), floor tuning that will not scale to a2r's 50-task plan, and our finding that exploration costs 2–3× when the source already succeeds. Prior art to beat: SAC's automatic temperature (a dual on entropy) and linear floor annealing.

posts.title: MoE环游记：2、不患寡而患不均 (MoE journey 2: the worry is unevenness, not scarcity)
posts.core_insight: The standard aux loss F·P (F = top-k load fractions, P = mean router probabilities) is usually stated without justification. Su derives it as the gradient-equivalent of ½‖F − Q‖² after the straight-through substitution F → P + sg[F − P], where the forward pass uses the hard statistic and the backward pass the smooth proxy: ∇½‖P + sg[F − P] − Q‖² = Σ(F_i − 1/n)∇P_i = ∇(F·P). That gives a general recipe for losses on non-differentiable statistics: write the loss in the hard statistic, then substitute P + sg[F − P]. The recipe also allows non-uniform targets Q, entropy versions (gradient Σ P_i log F_i) and unnormalised proxies. F·P itself is only a gradient surrogate; its minimum means nothing.
posts.rl_transfer: A recipe for auxiliary losses on behaviour statistics that PPO cannot differentiate. Examples: the per-task timeout fraction (in R212 ~60% of sweep eval episodes ran to timeout, a stall-to-avoid-failure mode under the −0.25 failure reward), the gripper-release rate, or the fraction of states where the deterministic mean and the noisy sample disagree on the gripper decision. Take hard F from rollouts and a smooth proxy P from the policy (e.g. Φ(μ_grip/σ)), with loss ½‖P + sg[F − P] − Q‖². But Su's own Loss-Free argument (10757) says such losses fight the main objective through shared parameters, so use them only where no isolated knob exists, e.g. a small STE term on the gripper mean during consolidation that pulls the deterministic release rate toward the stochastic one. Secondary value.

posts.title: MoE环游记：1、从几何意义出发 (MoE journey 1: starting from the geometry)
posts.core_insight: A dense FFN splits exactly into a sum of n expert vectors v_i = f(xW_i^A)W_i^B, and MoE asks to approximate Σ v_i with only k of them. If the v_i are mutually orthogonal, the best k are those with the largest norms, because large vectors cancel least. So the router should predict norms, ρ = h(xW^R) ≥ 0, the experts should be normalised directions e_i = v_i/‖v_i‖ (or RMSNorm with gain 1), and y = Σ_{i∈topk ρ} ρ_i e_i. This explains why multiplying ρ into the expert teaches correct ranking, why unnormalised router activations (sigmoid, ReLU) are fine and reduce competition when k > 1, and why sampling in proportion to norm is the variance-optimal sampled approximation.
posts.rl_transfer: Mostly a diagnostic link, not a recipe. Su's view explains our finding that training a gradient-importance subset of units is slower than full fine-tuning and no better than a random subset. A subset approximates the full update only when it is chosen per input and per step by contribution norm. Our importance and conflict scores are diffuse and unstable across steps, so any static subset behaves like a random one. The constructive version, a per-sample router that predicts which units' updates are largest (dynamic sparse fine-tuning), adds machinery the data say we do not need, since full FT + floor already wins. Not worth pursuing.

posts.title: 解构Scaling Law：优化、架构、数据的三重奏 (Deconstructing scaling laws: optimisation, architecture and data)
posts.core_insight: Su splits the loss on the ideal distribution into a data (generalisation) gap, an optimisation gap, an architecture gap and an irreducible remainder: L(E|D,A,O) = [L(E|D,A,O) − L(D|A,O)] + [L(D|A,O) − L(D|A,∞)] + [L(D|A,∞) − L(D|∞,∞)] + L(D|∞,∞). He models the optimisation gap as α1(Tη)^(−γ1) + α2·B^(−γ2) + α3·η^(γ3), with theory giving γ1 = γ3 = 1 and γ2 = 1/2, and minimises it with the 'different-power inequality' a·x^p + b·x^(−q) ≥ (p+q)(a^q b^p / (p^p q^q))^(1/(p+q)). This yields η* ∝ T^(−1/2), B* ∝ K^(1/2) for K samples seen, F* ∝ K^(−1/4), compute-optimal N* ∝ C^(3/7) and K* ∝ C^(4/7), and an optimal epoch count that grows as data shrink. Exponents encode the problem's difficulty and should be invariant under engineering; only coefficients move.
posts.rl_transfer: Useful as the evaluation frame of a recipe paper, not as a method. (1) Split time-to-90% into an exploration ('data') term, the steps until sustained training successes appear, and a consolidation ('optimisation') term, the steps from there to 90% deterministic eval. Our findings say the floor shrinks the first term and creates the second; a2r's 0.90 training EMA vs 0.53 eval on sweep pregrasp is the second term. Each recipe component should be shown to shrink a named term. (2) Su's universality argument gives a testable headline: floors and LR rules change coefficients, but reusing a source policy changes the problem, because the new task starts at its own seam. So fit steps-to-90% against the number of appended stages (Pick → Stack → …, insert → insert+turn) and test whether reuse changes the exponent. (3) Smaller points: for a fixed env-step budget the theory suggests batch (envs × horizon) ∝ √budget and an LR decaying like updates^(−1/2). PPO epochs and success replay play the role of multi-epoch training, which calls for more reuse when informative data (successes) are scarce; that supports self-imitation replay early on. Keep this analysis secondary to the method.

best_ideas: 1. Ignite, then consolidate (11782 + 11626, with 11833 as the evaluation frame). After reuse with a std floor, steps-to-90% are dominated by turning noisy successes into a reliable deterministic mean (our ManiSkill finding). a2r shows the same gap: sweep pregrasp training EMA 0.90 vs frozen eval 0.53 (E-10 O-219, unexplained). Keep the floor for behaviour and add a consolidation term for the mean. (a) Cheap version, quantile-gated self-imitation: an MSE pull of μθ(s) onto executed actions in each task's top-q advantage samples from successful episodes, with the threshold set to the EMA (1−q) quantile of the previous batch, q ≈ 5–10%, and a fixed budget per task. (b) Stronger version: add a privileged Q head with a Q-Prop/Taylor control variate, i.e. PPO on A − ⟨∇aQ(s,μ), a−μ⟩ plus −η·Q(s, μθ(s)); this gradient does not decay as w/σ² under a large floor. Report time-to-90% split into ignition and consolidation. Dev on ManiSkill Pick→Stack/Place with the current best arm (full FT + floor), then a2r insert_key insert→insert+turn. Kill if consolidation time does not drop at least 30% over 3 seeds. Touches no resets or SGS. Prior art: SIL, AWR, Q-Prop.

2. Loss-free exploration control (10757 + 10815 + 11760). Turn the std floor from a hand-tuned hyperparameter into a per-task dual variable φ_t, updated outside the gradient after each rollout with RMS-normalised steps. Before ignition, target a monotone exploration statistic: per-dimension entropy, or for gripper seams the share of episodes with at least one release event. After training success appears, target the stochastic–deterministic success gap, so the floor turns itself off. Predictions: it matches the best per-task floor without tuning (a2r needs 0.3 for hang and 0.6 for egg, and 1.0 is too slow), removes the 2–3× slowdown we see when the source already succeeds, scales to a2r's 50-task plan, and feeds idea 1's consolidation phase. Baselines: fixed floors {0.3, 0.6, 1.0}, linear anneal, SAC-style target-entropy dual. Dev on ManiSkill pairs where source success is about 0 and where it is high, then a2r hang and egg single-task.

3. Signal-aware trust-region allocation for joint PPO (11619 + 11626 + 11760 + 10815). (a) Replace per-task advantage std normalisation, which gives zero-success tasks unit-size noise updates, with A_t / max(S_t, S_min), where S_t is an EMA-histogram P95−P5 range of that task's returns. (b) Replace the single KL-adaptive LR with closed-form per-task loss weights w_t ← w_t·(δ/KL_t)^(λ/2) (λ ≈ 0.5, EMA 0.9, normalised to mean 1), plus proportional log-space control of the global LR. Motivation: the max-KL rule collapsed the LR to 2e-5–8e-5, against 4.4e-4–1e-3 single-task. With the mean rule, R212 still left sweep at 36.6/33.5% and egg at 12.9/14.8%; sweep only reached 94% in R217, with curricula and 720 min. Cheap first checks: a 'dead task' probe (add an impossible task to a ManiSkill joint run and see whether std-normalised noise erodes the other tasks), and single-task sweep at the joint run's per-task env-step budget to rule out a budget confound. Lower priority than ideas 1 and 2 because a2r has partly fixed this.

4. Norm-matched residual branch on a reused trunk (10945 + 11848). For stage extension and warm starts, add to the fully fine-tuned reused trunk a small task- or stage-routed residual branch (rank 8–32, RMSNorm before the up-projection). Set its output scale λ by norm matching at init: zero-init keeps the inherited mode and random re-init loses reuse. It targets a2r's warm-start failures, where tasks missing from the checkpoint inherit an inescapable hold or stall mode even with gripper floor 0.6 (R214, R216). It fits our ManiSkill finding that the new task lies 94–97% inside the old ~20-dim subspace. Kill if it does not beat full FT + floor on Pick→Stack in 3 seeds.

posts.title: From Parameter Symmetry to Effective Learning Rate
posts.core_insight: Exact single-parameter scale invariance, ℓ(w)=ℓ(c·w), almost never holds in pre-norm networks, but joint symmetries ℓ(c·w1, w2/c) are everywhere: Wq/Wk, Wv/Wo, up/down, and a norm's γ with the matrices it feeds. Requiring the update to be covariant, ϕ(c1·w, c2·g) = c1·ϕ(w, g) (the trajectory must not depend on how scale is split between symmetric parameters or on rescaling the loss), forces ϕ = ||w||·F(w/||w||, g/||g||). The simplest instance is w ← w − η·||w||·u/||u||, so η is the effective learning rate (ELR), the relative step ||Δw||/||w||. For AdamW the ELR schedule implied by linear decay is (1−t/T)/sqrt(1−c0·e^(−c1·t)): high start, fast early fall, near-linear later. [kexue.fm was unreachable: WebFetch got 403 then connection refused, local curl timed out. Read via the community English machine translation at rohin-garg.github.io/kexue-en.]
posts.rl_transfer: Two concrete uses. (1) ELR at reuse and after unlocks. In a2r's pre-LN ResBlocks (LN→SiLU→Linear1→LN→SiLU→Linear2), each Linear1 plus its bias is exactly scale-invariant because a LayerNorm follows it. The input projection and all Linear2s form one joint-scale group because the trunk ends in a LayerNorm. Under Adam these norms only grow, so ELR = lr·||Δw||/||w|| decays over a long curriculum and is already low in a reused checkpoint. Log per-layer ELR on a long a2r run and at the start of reuse fine-tunes. If it has dropped more than about 3×, rescale Linear1 (and its bias) to its init norm at reuse or unlock time; the policy stays exactly the same, but reset Adam's moments. The alternative, projecting after every step (Hyperball), is already published for RL as NaP (Lyle et al. 2024) and SimbaV2, so it is a component, not a contribution. (2) Covariance across tasks and action dims. The PPO mean gradient scales as 1/σ, and a2r's per-task KL is Σ_j Δμ_j²/2σ_j². So per-task or per-dim std silently re-weights tasks on the shared trunk and inside the KL-adaptive LR. A covariant update measures each task in its own σ-units (best idea 3).

posts.title: A New Understanding of Momentum: Approximating Gradient Descent at the Feature Level
posts.core_insight: For a layer Y = XW, choose the update Φ so the feature change XΦ matches the feature gradient. Minimising ½||XΦ − ∂L/∂Y||² + ½λ||Φ||² gives Φ* = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹·G: the ordinary gradient multiplied by the inverse of the ridge-regularised input covariance, a 'more reliable gradient'. Taking EMAs of G (the momentum M) and of XᵀX (Z) gives W ← W − η·Z⁻¹M; Newton-Muon applies msign to Z⁻¹M. Solving the same regression with one gradient step per iteration instead gives DeltaMomentum, Φ_t = (1−γλ)Φ_{t−1} + γ(G_t − X_tᵀX_t·Φ_{t−1}), a delta rule with no matrix inverse. Isotropic inputs or λ→∞ recover SGDM/Muon. The costs: the optimizer needs the activations, and an input-based preconditioner confines movement to span(X), so λ must be tuned. [Source: English machine translation; kexue.fm unreachable.]
posts.rl_transfer: Apply it only to the Gaussian action head μ = h·W (512→7 in a2r, 256→act_dim in our ManiSkill MLP). The PPO surrogate gives a per-state desired mean shift D = −A·(a−μ)/σ², and (HᵀH/B + λI)⁻¹HᵀD is the least-squares fit of that shift onto the features. Implementation: one Cholesky solve per minibatch with Z = EMA(HᵀH/B) (512×512, negligible cost). Scale column j by σ_j²; this makes it the exact natural gradient of the head, because the Gaussian-mean Fisher is HᵀH ⊗ diag(1/σ²). Size the step to a fixed head-KL budget, KL = ½·mean_s Σ_j (h(s)·ΔW_j)²/σ_j². Keep Adam and the KL controller for the trunk. This targets today's slow phase, turning noisy successes under the std floor into a reliable deterministic mean. It also targets our probe result that features occupy ~20 of 256 dims with the new task 94–97% inside them. Raw gradients move the low-variance feature directions, such as those that separate release states from carry states, slower in proportion to their eigenvalue, and they leak the change into similar states; whitening equalises the directions. Follow Su's caveat that input preconditioning limits exploration: start with a large λ and anneal it. Prior art is ACKTR/K-FAC and natural PG, so the claim must be the consolidation step of the reuse recipe, not a new optimizer.

posts.title: Why does the official Muon have an extra max(1, ·) compared to the MuP version?
posts.core_insight: Choose the scale α in ΔW = η·α·msign(M) so every feature change satisfies ||x·ΔW||_RMS = η·||x||_RMS. For d_in ≤ d_out this holds exactly with α = sqrt(d_out/d_in). For d_in > d_out it depends on the input: isotropic x gives ≈ ||x||_RMS, so α = 1, while anisotropic x approaches the worst case sqrt(d_in/d_out)·||x||_RMS, which needs α = sqrt(d_out/d_in). Hence the official α = sqrt(max(1, d_out/d_in)) fits early training (isotropic features), the MuP α fits mid and late training, and Su suggests α = sqrt(max(τ_t, d_out/d_in)) with τ_t decaying from 1 to 0. [Source: English machine translation; kexue.fm unreachable.]
posts.rl_transfer: Policy and value heads are the extreme d_in ≫ d_out case: 512→7 action head and 512→1 value head in a2r. Extending Su's argument to inputs that are isotropic inside an r-dimensional subspace gives ||x·Φ||_RMS ≈ sqrt(d_in/r)·||x||_RMS, so the right head scale is α ≈ sqrt(max(d_out, r)/d_in). With our probe's r ≈ 20 of 256, a spectrally normalised head step moves the action about 3.6× more than the isotropic estimate assumes. The effect is larger for a trained, anisotropic source than for a fresh net; Adam's sign-like step behaves similarly when G is low-rank. Consequence: during reuse the head can dominate the measured KL, so a2r's KL-adaptive LR (kl_target 0.01) or our target_kl early stop throttles the trunk. Cheap test: on reuse fine-tunes, split each minibatch's KL into the part from a head-only update and the part from a trunk-only update. If the head dominates, give it an LR multiplier sqrt(max(d_out, r_eff)/d_in), recomputed each iteration from the feature spectrum, and let the controller raise the global LR.

posts.title: Beyond MuP: 4. Adhering to Parameter Stability
posts.core_insight: To keep a parameter norm bounded (||ω|| ≤ τ) with minimal interference, use the minimal-change projection argmin over ||ω̃|| ≤ τ of ||ω − ω̃||_RMS. Apply it either after each step (Post Clip) or before each step with a shrinking radius (Pre Decay: project ω_{t−1} to radius (1−η)·||ω_{t−1}||, then subtract η·φ_t). Pre Decay guarantees ||ω_t|| ≤ max(||ω_0||, τ) from the triangle inequality alone. Under the RMS/Frobenius norm, Pre Decay is exactly ordinary weight decay. Under the spectral norm, Post Clip is singular-value clipping, U·min(Σ, τ)·Vᵀ, and Pre Decay is spectral weight decay, W ← W − η·λ·σ1·u1·v1ᵀ; both can be approximated by clipping only the top singular value (power iteration) each step. Plain weight decay can also bound the spectral norm, but only by over-intervening on every singular value. [Source: English machine translation; kexue.fm unreachable.]
posts.rl_transfer: Our exploration floor is a clip implemented the non-minimal way. a2r computes std = max(exp(log_std), min_std) in the forward pass, and our ManiSkill agent clamps logstd in the forward pass. Once the learned log-std dips below the floor its gradient is exactly zero, and after Adam's momentum dies out it stays frozen in a dead zone. From then on the policy can never raise σ above the floor, yet the Stack 'ignition' needed the gripper std to grow from 0.6 to 1.4. Su's minimal-change projection is the fix: use σ = exp(log_std) in the forward pass and project the parameter after every optimizer step, log_std ← max(log_std, log floor). a2r already does exactly this for its [−3, 0] clamp. It is a one-line change. Diagnostic: if the raw logged log-std sits just below log(floor) for most of a run, the dead zone is active. Hypothesis to test on 3–5 seeds of Pick→Stack: the projection floor removes part of what we filed as seed luck in whether a run ignites. Secondary: if long teacher runs get a norm bound, prefer top-singular clipping or spectral decay, so the low-rank old-skill subspace is not uniformly shrunk.

posts.title: Beyond MuP: 3. Special Cases, Special Treatment
posts.core_insight: Applying the three stability metrics layer by layer gives a steepest-descent rule for each layer type. Embedding: row-wise normalised SGD, ΔE_i = −η·G_i/||G_i||_RMS. Output head: it must be 'responsible for the loss', so its metrics are taken on the cross-entropy itself, bounded by |LSE(a) − LSE(b)| ≤ max_i |a_i − b_i|. That yields column-wise normalised SGD scaled by 1/d, ΔW_{:,i} = −(η/d)·G_{:,i}/||G_{:,i}||_RMS, with init variance 1/d². RMSNorm γ, viewed as a diagonal matrix, gets SignSGD; biases get normalised SGD; Muon is only for hidden dense matrices. [Source: English machine translation; kexue.fm unreachable.]
posts.rl_transfer: Repeat the derivation for the Gaussian policy head, which is also responsible for the loss. Changing μ_j by Δμ_j changes log π by ε_j·Δμ_j/σ_j and the KL by Δμ_j²/2σ_j², so the head's update-stability metric is max_j |Δμ_j|/σ_j. Steepest descent under that metric is a per-output-column normalised step scaled by that dimension's std (per task when log-std is per task): ΔW_{:,j} = −η·σ_j·G_{:,j}/||G_{:,j}||. Adam instead moves μ by a fixed amount in action units, which is 1/σ slower in σ-units. Raising the gripper floor from 0.3 to 0.6 therefore halves how fast the gripper mean moves relative to its own noise. That is a concrete candidate mechanism for 'training success rises but the deterministic mean lags'. Test in ManiSkill: same floor, σ-scaled head step vs Adam head; metrics are the stochastic-vs-deterministic success gap and time to 90% deterministic success. The same rule removes the per-dim and per-task imbalance in the KL that drives a2r's adaptive LR. Also treat the PointNet point-wise first layer as embedding-like: keep it on Adam or normalised SGD, not Muon.

posts.title: Beyond MuP: 2. Linear Layers and Steepest Descent
posts.core_insight: With an input norm (pre-norm and post-norm both normalise the input of each sublayer), y = Norm(x)·W has forward stability sqrt(d_in/d_out)·||W||_2 and update stability sqrt(d_in/d_out)·||ΔW||_2. Requiring both to be Θ(1) gives a spectral init with std ∝ sqrt(d_out/d_in)/(sqrt(d_in)+sqrt(d_out)). Steepest descent under that budget, minimising tr(GᵀΔW) subject to ||ΔW||_2 ≤ η·sqrt(d_out/d_in), gives ΔW = −η·sqrt(d_out/d_in)·msign(G), the MuP version of Muon (via the nuclear-norm dual). Without a norm layer Muon stays roughly valid as long as ||x||_RMS is about constant. [Source: English machine translation; kexue.fm unreachable.]
posts.rl_transfer: a2r's trunk (Linear(n_in, 512), then two pre-LN ResBlocks, then LN and SiLU) satisfies the input-norm premise, so its 512×512 matrices are the legitimate place for a spectral (Muon) update. The PointNet point-wise layers, the 7-d action head, the value head, log_std and the LN γ/β are not. If we test Muon in PPO, restrict it to those matrices and keep the KL controller setting η. Use the spectral init above for any new trunk layers, for example when growing or unsharing parameters. The hypothesis worth a cheap test is in multi-task joint training: msign gives every singular direction of the summed task gradient Σ_k G_k the same step, so weak tasks are not drowned out (see 10592). Do not expect it to be a recipe-level contribution on its own.

posts.title: MuP之上：1. 好模型的三个特征 (Beyond MuP 1: Three Characteristics of a Good Model)
posts.core_insight: A good model needs three Θ(1) quantities, each the RMS of an output with a sup over inputs. Forward stability: max over x of ||f(x;ω)||_RMS. Dependency stability: max over x1, x2 of ||f(x1;ω) − f(x2;ω)||_RMS, so the output really depends on the input. Update stability: max over x of ||f(x;ω+Δω) − f(x;ω)||_RMS, which is what constrains the optimizer. f can be a layer, a block or the whole model. Su prefers sup to expectation because it needs no input distribution, is invariant to monotone transforms and protects the worst case. [Source: Wayback snapshot of the Chinese original.]
posts.rl_transfer: For a policy, update stability is the per-state change per update (Δμ/σ, or the per-state KL). PPO and a2r instead control a batch-mean KL; a2r takes per-task means and reduces them by max or by mean. After an unlock, states from mastered stages are a small fraction of the batch. The mean KL can then sit at 0.01 while those states move a lot, which fits 'the unlock curriculum wipes learned stages'. Diagnostic: each iteration, log the 95th–99th percentile of per-state KL on a fixed probe set of states from already-mastered stages, and check whether wipe-outs coincide with spikes. Caveat: the lab already found that a max over noisy per-task KL estimates is biased upward and collapsed the LR to about 3e-5. So use an EMA'd quantile rather than a raw max, and use it as a monitor or as the trigger for a targeted post-hoc fix (see 11126), not as an anchor; KL-to-source anchoring already failed in our G3′ test. Dependency stability also suggests a cheap interference monitor: the policy's sensitivity to the task/stage input.

posts.title: Is the optimal Adam hyperparameter β1 = β2?
posts.core_insight: With β1 = β2 = β the bias-corrected moments are matched weighted averages, so v̂ = m̂² + σ̂²: the second moment is the squared EMA mean plus the EMA variance. The Adam step is then u = sign(m̂)/sqrt(1 + σ̂²/m̂²): each coordinate is bounded by 1 and shrunk by the inverse signal-to-noise ratio, an 'SNR-aware sign descent'. Conversely, choosing β2 to maximise the worst-case v̂ for a given m̂ (Cauchy–Schwarz twice) gives β2 = β1, the only choice that guarantees v̂ ≥ m̂². β2 > β1 still suits small-batch, noisy regimes. [Source: English machine translation; kexue.fm unreachable.]
posts.rl_transfer: a2r uses Adam(0.9, 0.999). v̂ averages over about 1000 steps, roughly 50 PPO iterations at the default 5 epochs × 4 minibatches. So after an unlock, a new task joining, or a reward change, it carries stale gradient scales for tens of iterations. Try β1 = β2 (0.9/0.9 or 0.95/0.95) on the actor. Coordinates whose minibatch gradients flip sign from step to step are then shrunk automatically while consistent coordinates keep full steps; sign flipping is exactly how we measured multi-task conflict ('diffuse across units, unstable over steps'). It is a one-flag change; test it on the 10-task joint run and right after unlocks. It is already known in RL (β1 = β2 against PPO policy collapse in Dohare et al. 2023; Adam-Rel by Ellis et al. 2024 resets Adam's timestep each iteration), so it is a recipe component, not a contribution. It does not stop pure-noise random walks: with zero signal, |u| is still about sqrt((1−β)/(1+β)) ≈ 0.23.

posts.title: Why do we prefer isotropy? An understanding based on steepest descent
posts.core_insight: Under parameter gradient descent the features change by ΔY = −η·XXᵀ·∂L/∂Y: the desired feature gradient filtered by the batch Gram matrix. So steepest descent on the parameters equals steepest descent on the features only when XXᵀ ≈ I, that is, when the inputs are isotropic. Whitening, X(XᵀX)^(−1/2), is the exact fix, and BN, IN, LN and RMSNorm are cheap diagonal or per-sample approximations of it. With Muon, isotropic inputs give ΔY ≈ −η·msign(∂L/∂Y), so spectral steepest descent holds at both levels. [Source: English machine translation; kexue.fm unreachable.]
posts.rl_transfer: Read XXᵀ over a batch of states as the last layer's tangent kernel. A PPO update driven by advantages at some states moves the action at every state with overlapping features, weighted by h(s)·h(s′). Our probe (old-task features in ~20 of 256 dims, new task 94–97% inside) says this kernel is low-rank and shared across stages. That predicts two things: slow consolidation at rare seam states, and new-stage updates leaking into old-stage behaviour (the unlock wipe-out). Diagnostic: per update, measure leakage = ||Δμ on an old-stage probe set|| / ||Δμ on new-stage states||, plus the spectrum of HᵀH. Fix candidates: the whitened head from 11875, or a ZCA whitening layer before the head. Recompute that layer each PPO iteration with shrinkage and fold it into the head weights so the policy does not change at the moment of recomputation. a2r's LayerNorm→SiLU features share a large common mean (SiLU ≥ −0.28), so centre them before whitening.

posts.title: Muon优化器指南：快速上手与关键细节 (Muon Optimizer Guide: Quick Start and Key Details)
posts.core_insight: Four Muon variants differ only in the factor in front of msign: naive 1; Keller Jordan sqrt(max(1, d_out/d_in)); MuP sqrt(d_out/d_in); Moonlight 0.2·sqrt(max(d_in, d_out)). The Moonlight factor matches Adam's update RMS, so Adam's LR and weight decay can be reused; the other three need about 0.2·sqrt(d), roughly 10×, Adam's LR. d_in and d_out follow the layer's semantics (torch nn.Linear stores (out, in)); Muon is only for dense-input hidden matrices, while embeddings, output heads and 1-D parameters stay on Adam, and conv kernels are reshaped to (k·k·d_in, d_out). Expect Muon to be about equal to or slightly better than Adam; a large gap either way usually means a setup error. [Source: Wayback snapshot of the Chinese original.]
posts.rl_transfer: Practical recipe if we test Muon in PPO. Use the Moonlight scale so a2r's KL-adaptive LR range (1e-5 to 1e-3), kl_target 0.01 and max_grad 1.0 carry over unchanged. Put Muon on the 512×512 ResBlock matrices and the n_in→512 projection, and keep Adam for the PointNet point-wise layers, the action and value heads, log_std and the LayerNorm parameters. Get the (out, in) orientation of nn.Linear right. Our ManiSkill 256-wide Tanh MLP has no input norm, so add LayerNorm before testing there. Its value is as a cheap ablation tool for the multi-task and train-for-reuse hypotheses (10592, 10739), not as the paper's contribution.

posts.title: Muon续集：为什么我们选择尝试Muon？ (Muon Sequel: Why We Chose to Try Muon)
posts.core_insight: An optimizer step is a 'least action' problem: minimise tr(GᵀΔW) subject to a stability measure ρ(ΔW) ≤ η. Because ||x·ΔW|| ≤ ||ΔW||_2·||x|| is the tightest bound on the output change, choosing ρ = spectral norm gives ΔW = −η·msign(G), which is Muon. At scale Muon needs weight decay, which bounds ||W_t||_2 ≤ max(||W_0||_2, 1/λ). Matching Adam's update RMS (Φ·0.2·sqrt(max(n,m))) transfers Adam's hyperparameters, and Moonlight reached about 2× the compute efficiency of Adam. Muon-trained weights have higher singular-value entropy, and switching optimizers between pre-training and fine-tuning (Adam→Muon or Muon→Adam) is suboptimal. [Source: Wayback snapshot of the Chinese original.]
posts.rl_transfer: Two links to the reuse thread. (1) Train sources for reuse. Our Adam-trained Pick source uses about 20 of 256 hidden dims. A Muon-trained source should have higher singular-value entropy, H(σ) = −Σ p_i·log p_i / log n with p_i = σ_i²/Σσ_j². Cheap ManiSkill test: train Pick to 90% with Adam and with Muon, record H(σ) and the feature effective rank, then run the identical reuse + floor fine-tune to Stack and Place and compare steps to 90%. (2) The optimizer-mismatch finding says not to switch optimizers at reuse time: fine-tune an Adam-trained a2r teacher with Adam, and run Adam→Muon only as a control. H(σ) of the trunk is also a cheap monitor for representation collapse after unlocks.

posts.title: Muon优化器赏析：从向量到矩阵的本质跨越 (Appreciating Muon: The Essential Leap from Vectors to Matrices)
posts.core_insight: Muon: M_t = β·M_{t−1} + G_t and W ← W − η·[msign(M_t) + λ·W], where msign(M) = U·Vᵀ = M·(MᵀM)^(−1/2) is the matrix sign, computed by a Newton–Schulz quintic with coefficients about (3.4445, −4.7750, 2.0315). It is invariant to loss scaling and sets every singular value of the update to 1, the matrix analogue of sign: a diagonal M gives SignSGD and an n×1 M gives L2 normalisation. It is steepest descent under the spectral norm, because the maximum of tr(GᵀΦ) over ||Φ||_2 = 1 is the nuclear norm Σσ_i, attained at Φ = msign(G); Shampoo with β = 0 gives the same update. [Source: Wayback snapshot of the Chinese original.]
posts.rl_transfer: Multi-task angle. The shared trunk's gradient G = Σ_k G_k has its top singular directions set by the tasks with the largest gradients: high-signal tasks and, with per-task log-std, small-σ tasks, since the mean gradient scales as 1/σ_k. Adam and SGD therefore mostly follow the dominant tasks. msign(G) gives every singular direction the same step, so directions carried by weak tasks (low-success tasks, upstream start types) are not drowned out, with no explicit per-task gradient surgery. Test on a2r's 10-task joint config: Muon on the trunk vs Adam under the same KL controller, comparing per-task success and the alone-vs-joint gap. Risk: it also amplifies pure-noise directions from pre-success tasks, so pair it with the zero-success masking in best idea 2.

posts.title: 为什么梯度裁剪的默认模长是1？ (Why Is the Default Gradient-Clipping Norm 1?)
posts.core_insight: To first order a step changes the loss by ΔL ≈ −η·u·g. For SGD this is ΔL = −η·||g||², and stable training (per-step loss changes well below η) implies ||g|| < 1 in the long run, which is why τ = 1 separates normal steps from outliers at any model size; large early gradients call for warmup. Su proposes capping the learning rate by the predicted loss change, η_t = η·min(1, T/(u_t·g_t)). For sign-like Adam, ΔL = −η·||g||_1 = −η·sqrt(N)·||g||·cos(sign g, g), which implies η ∝ 1/sqrt(N). [Source: Wayback snapshot of the Chinese original.]
posts.rl_transfer: PPO's KL-adaptive LR is reactive: a2r multiplies or divides it by 1.5 per minibatch after measuring the step's KL, with kl_target 0.01. The predictive analogue: before stepping, compute the exact second-order KL of the proposed update for the Gaussian policy, KL ≈ ½·mean_s Σ_j (J_μ(s)·Δθ)_j²/σ_j², using one forward-mode JVP per minibatch. Then set η_t = min(η, sqrt(2δ/(uᵀFu))), per task if wanted. This gives exact per-task KLs without the noisy-max bias the lab hit. It is essentially TRPO's step-size rule applied to Adam's direction, so novelty is low, but it removes LR collapse and oscillation in 10-task joint runs. Also check a2r's max_grad = 1.0: with equal-weight per-task losses and per-task advantage normalisation the global gradient norm changes with the number of tasks, so the clip may bind differently in joint and single-task runs.

posts.title: 从谱范数梯度到新式权重衰减的思考 (From the Spectral-Norm Gradient to a New Weight Decay)
posts.core_insight: Since ||W||_2 = u1ᵀ·W·v1, its gradient is u1·v1ᵀ (when σ1 > σ2), so the gradient of ½||W||_2² is σ1·u1·v1ᵀ = W·v1·v1ᵀ, the best rank-1 approximation of W. Spectral weight decay, W ← W − λ·W·v1·v1ᵀ, therefore penalises only the largest singular value (Frobenius decay shrinks all of them), controls the output scale just enough, and costs about 10 power iterations x ← WᵀWx/||WᵀWx||; Su saw at most a marginal gain on language models. [Source: Wayback snapshot of the Chinese original.]
posts.rl_transfer: No transfer to our main pain points: a2r's PPO uses plain Adam without weight decay. Optional uses: if long teacher or curriculum runs need a norm bound, decay only the top singular direction so the old skill's low-rank subspace is not uniformly shrunk. Or bound the trunk's Lipschitz constant to make the privileged teacher smoother and easier for the RGB-D student to imitate in DAgger. That second use could cost precision on mm-scale insertion and would need its own test.

posts.title: Adam的epsilon如何影响学习率的Scaling Law？ (How Adam's ε Affects the Learning-Rate Scaling Law)
posts.core_insight: Adam's ε turns sign into softsign(x, ε) = x/sqrt(x² + ε²), which interpolates between SignSGD (ε → 0) and SGD (ε → ∞, where ε·softsign → x). With per-coordinate gradient noise g + σ·z/sqrt(B), the expected step is about softsign(g_i, ε)/sqrt(1 + πκ²/2B). The second moment is about ν_i²β² + (1 − β²), so the optimal LR is about β·Σν_i·g_i divided by (β²·Σν_iν_j·H_ij + (1−β²)·ΣH_ii). A larger ε makes the 'surge', where the optimal LR falls as batch size grows, less likely and pushes the scaling toward SGD's. ε matters once typical per-coordinate gradients approach it, as in large models and late training. [Source: Wayback snapshot of the Chinese original.]
posts.rl_transfer: With sparse reward and per-task normalised advantages, Adam's tiny ε (1e-8 in a2r, 1e-5 in our ManiSkill code) turns pure noise into steps as large as signal steps (update RMS about 0.2·η). This happens before the first success, or for any task or start type with no successes yet. It is the 'pre-success random walk on critic noise that erodes unanchored skills' we observed. Setting ε near the gradient noise floor (per coordinate, ε_i ≈ sqrt(EMA of the minibatch variance of g_i)) makes Adam a soft SNR gate: sign-like where signal ≫ noise, SGD-like and small where the gradient is noise. Wherever ε dominates the step scale becomes η/ε, so retune the LR. Quick sweep: ε ∈ {1e-8, 1e-6, 1e-4, 1e-3} × LR on the reuse fine-tune, measuring source-skill retention before the first success and time to 90%. Cruder than the explicit gate in best idea 2, but it is a single hyperparameter.

posts.title: 当Batch Size增大时，学习率该如何随之变化？ (How Should the Learning Rate Change as Batch Size Grows?)
posts.core_insight: Square-root (variance-matching) and linear (SDE) scaling of LR with batch size are only local approximations. Minimising the second-order expected loss after one step gives η* = η_max/(1 + B_noise/B), with η_max = gᵀg/gᵀHg and B_noise = tr(ΣH)/gᵀHg, approximated by the gradient noise scale B_simple = tr(Σ)/|g|². The steps–data trade-off follows: (S/S_min − 1)·(E/E_min − 1) = 1. For sign-like Adam the expected sign is about sign(g)/sqrt(1 + πκ²/2B), so η* ∝ sqrt(B) at small B, and off-diagonal Hessian terms can make η* fall again beyond B_noise (the 'surge'). [Source: Wayback snapshot of the Chinese original.]
posts.rl_transfer: Estimate B_simple every PPO iteration from the spread of the minibatch gradients we already compute. Our ManiSkill code has 32 minibatches per epoch; a2r's 4 are too few, so split them into chunks or use an EMA. Estimate per task or start-type group and per parameter group (actor vs critic). Two uses. (i) An SNR-gated actor step: lr_actor = lr_KL·B/(B + B_simple), the noise-scale gain (McCandlish et al. 2018; compare AdaScale). With no success signal the policy then barely moves. This replaces KL-to-source anchoring as the way to protect a reused skill, and it stops new-stage critic noise from overwriting mastered stages after an unlock. (ii) A test of when the exploration floor pays: the floor should help only if it lowers B_simple, adding more signal than variance. That matches our finding that exploration helps only when the source's success on the target is ~0 and costs 2–3× when it is already high. First check whether B_simple measured with and without the floor separates PushRetreat/Stack from the high-success pairs; if it does not, drop the controller.

posts.title: QK-Clip：让Muon在Scaleup之路上更进一步 (QK-Clip: Taking Muon Further on the Road to Scale-Up)
posts.core_insight: MaxLogit, S_max = max q_i·k_j, is bounded by ||x_i||·||x_j||·||W_q||·||W_k||, so its growth signals exploding spectral norms of W_q and W_k; indirect fixes (lower LR, more weight decay, softcap, partial QK-norm) all failed. QK-Clip uses the monitored quantity itself: after each optimizer step, if a head's S_max exceeds τ, multiply that head's W_qc and W_kc by sqrt(τ/S_max), and W_qr by τ/S_max because the shared k_r must not be touched. Clipping is per head, because per-layer clipping over-shrank 'innocent' heads; in Kimi K2 (τ = 100) it was active from about 7k to 70k steps, after which MaxLogit stayed below τ on its own. Su attributes the blow-up to Muon's full-rank updates colliding with existing singular directions, which also explains why Adam↔Muon pretrain/fine-tune mixing is suboptimal, and generalises the idea to 'clip exactly where it is unstable' with the smallest post-hoc weight change. [Source: Wayback snapshot of the Chinese original.]
posts.rl_transfer: a2r's joint-training collapse is the per-layer-versus-per-head over-clipping case. One global adaptive LR, driven by the max of 10 noisy per-task KLs, throttled every task; the LR fell to about 3e-5. The lab's mean-KL fix stops the throttling but lets the most sensitive task overshoot its budget, for example the one with the smallest σ_k or one that has already converged. QK-Clip's recipe: keep the global LR on the mean KL, and add a per-task correction triggered by each task's own EMA KL, so only the offender is slowed ('哪里不稳Clip哪里'). Options: (a) a per-task loss weight for the next minibatches, w_k = min(1, kl_target/EMA KL_k); (b) per-task early stopping, dropping task k's samples from the remaining epochs once its KL exceeds 2·kl_target; (c) rescaling only task k's own log-std row. This is a per-iteration PPO trust region, not a KL-to-source anchor (which failed in G3′), and it touches no resets, start states or SGS. Test: ManiSkill 4–6-task joint PPO with per-task log-std, then a2r 10-task joint against the lab's mean-KL baseline; metrics are per-task steps to 90% and the alone-vs-joint gap.

best_ideas: 1. Natural-gradient action head as the consolidation step of reuse (11875, 11549, 11647, 11772). Problem: under the exploration floor, training success rises while the deterministic mean lags or collapses, and the source's features sit in ~20 of 256 dims. Two mechanisms make this slow. Adam moves μ a fixed amount in action units, which is 1/σ slower relative to the noise. Raw gradients update low-variance feature directions slower in proportion to their eigenvalue and leak the change into similar states; those are exactly the directions that separate seam/release states from carry states.
